# Use Case Diagram

Figure 2 lists the adjustments made to the original use case diagram (Figure 1). This includes the removal of signing up and creating an account as a sub-use case for the base use cases.  This was amended as the process of signing up is considered a precondition, not a step within the operational flow of the other base use cases.

Initial Diagram. Furthermore, a superactor “User” was added which the primary actors  “Jobseeker” and “Employer” inherit from and have an “is-a” relationship with.

Job seekers interact with the system to discover and manage suitable ad-hoc job opportunities. Their three base use cases include setting preferences, indicating availability, and cancelling their shift. For the Employer, their three base use cases   
are listing jobs, rating employees, and cancelling their shifts.

# Initial Diagrams

Figure 3 lists all the classes contained within the “Model” layer in the MVC model (Model, Views, Controller). The diagrams highlight the cardinalities and the different relationships between classes, namely inheritance or association. The diagram also lists the different attributes and methods called within each class. These will form the basis for the organisation of data within our back-end.

There are 9 classes listed: User, Client, JobSeeker, Preferences, Availability, Shifts, Assignment, Feedback and Payouts.

# Sequence Diagram Diagrams

Building on the use cases, sequence diagrams were created to showcase the sequential interactions between the different classes. There are 8 sequence diagrams listed below:

* Creating an account (Figure 4\)   
* Authentication (Figure 5\)  
* Jobseeker Indicates Availability  (Figure 6\)  
* Cancel Shift Diagram  (Figure 7\)  
* Preferences  (Figure 8\)  
* Lists Jobs  (Figure 9\)  
* Review Employee  (Figure 10\)  
* Employer Cancels Job Listing  (Figure 11\)
